title: Tears, Toil and Fading Fame
overview: The writer looks at oppression, envy, lonely overwork and fickle crowds, finds a bright spot in companionship, and still ends by calling it all a chasing after the wind.

parts.label: Tears with no comforter (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The writer sees people crushed by those with power, weeping with no one willing to stand beside them. He says bluntly that the dead, and even those never born, are better off, an honest cry of despair that the text does not soften.

parts.label: Work, envy and enough (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Verse 4 can be read two ways: hard work springs from rivalry with the neighbor, or the successful worker simply ends up envied by the neighbor, and either way he calls it chasing the wind. Yet the lazy person who folds his hands ruins himself too, so he praises a middle path: one handful with peace beats two fists full with strain.

parts.label: The lonely workaholic (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: A man with no child or brother works without end and is never satisfied with his money. He finally asks who all this is for and why he denies himself any joy, and the writer calls it a miserable business.

parts.label: Two are better than one (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: In contrast to the lonely man, companions lift each other up when they fall, keep each other warm on cold nights, and defend each other from attack. The cord of three strands seems to be a saying about how bonds grow stronger the more lives are woven together.

parts.label: The fickle crowd (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: A poor but teachable young man is better than an old king who will no longer listen, and the crowds rush to follow the new ruler, yet later generations are not pleased with him either, so even power and popularity are chasing the wind. Scholars are unsure whether a real king is meant, and older attempts to link it to events after Solomon's reign are guesses.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether bleak lines like the dead being better off reflect the writer's settled view or a deliberately limited view of life 'under the sun' that the book means to challenge.
think: When you look at what you work hardest for, who or what is it really for?
